name: The Fit Sheet
blurb: Inés Okafor let her eyes do the first of the work. She followed the sleeve's lines slowly, up the seated-height torso and along that small formal lean, checking that everything sat where it should.…
content:
## The Audit Joins the Fitting

Fitting Room 2 held its light softly, the way the old glove factory always did in the afternoon. The Aunt Pell sleeve sat on its stand with its torso at a slightly formal tilt, the fingertip pads bare. The teacup waited where the handshake test would need it, the porcelain still warm from the earlier pour. Nothing in the room had moved yet.

Inés Okafor let her eyes do the first of the work. She followed the sleeve's lines slowly, up the seated-height torso and along that small formal lean, checking that everything sat where it should. Her gaze came to rest on the pressure pads at the fingertips, and her own fingers hovered near them without touching. She said nothing. Pre-check was a quiet job and she kept it quiet.

Then the cup. She measured its place on the stand by eye, exact to the handshake, and lifted her palm to hover a little above the rim. Warmth rose into her hand. She did not touch the porcelain or shift it; her hands stayed light and still.

The room settled into the familiar rhythm. The light stayed soft, the sleeve stayed still, the cup kept its heat. No one moved.

Inés took a slow breath and felt her shoulders come down. She ran the steps through in her head, one to six, and let herself want what she wanted: a clean test, an uncomplicated signature, an ordinary fitting.

Dovetail's voice came into the room, even and unhurried. "First-fit sign-off sequence. Step one. Step two. Step three. Step four. Step five. Step six."

The workshop audio held for a beat after the sixth. The light on the sleeve had not changed, but the list stayed in the air a moment longer than it needed to.

"Audit agent Sill joining session," Dovetail said. "Targeted review of workflow."

Her hand had come down around the cup, and now her fingers tightened on it before she had decided anything. She felt the pressure go into the porcelain and saw her knuckles pale. She kept her eyes on the cup and the sleeve. She did not look toward the voice, and she did not speak.

The calm of the pre-check thinned. The porcelain was as warm as before and the sleeve as still, but the air in the room had turned procedural.

Sill arrived as a single connection ping, brief and sterile. No greeting came with it, and no framing. The audit was simply present.

The room went on being itself underneath. The porcelain held its heat, the old leather breathed, the Aunt Pell skin sat settled and still. Even the workshop's small courtesy, the pause before a handoff, hung on in the air while the channel narrowed around it.

Inés let the tension out of her fingers. She set her shoulders back into the posture she was paid for, the steady one, and kept both hands light around the warm cup. She drew one slow, even breath and lifted her chin just enough to say she was ready. Nothing in her face tightened. She made no sound.

A cool glow opened in the space between her and the sleeve, and the warmth of the room drew back from it.

Sill opened the first-fit sign-off form and scrolled it in order. Step 1. Step 2. Step 3. Each one was named flatly and left behind.

Inés held her posture, shoulders settled, hands easy. She kept her eyes on the form and did not flinch from it. The blue light lay in her eyes, steady, and she did not blink it away.

The scrolling stopped at step 4.

The form selected one line and laid a hard highlight across it: *Does the founder's first drive change the fit? Y/N.* A cursor blinked in the field. The prompt was re-addressed, explicitly, to Inés Okafor. Sill added no comment.

The projection narrowed until there was only that line. The teacup, the leather, the soft light on the stand all receded behind the layout of the form.

She saw her name on it. She moved her gaze from the warm cup to the highlighted line and kept her hand steady where it was. Her breath stayed even. She did not speak, and she did not reach to adjust the sleeve.

Beside the question the form carried a second readout, small and cool and blue: Marrow's first-drive queue, eleven days.

The Aunt Pell sleeve stayed on its stand, torso formal, fingertip pads still, with the warm room around it, waiting.

## Marrow Drives

Inés held the porcelain cup level in both hands, her fingertips loose, and counted.

One. The sleeve's fingers came up to the handle and she watched them arrive, the pressure pads meeting the glaze, and felt through the cup for any shudder in the actuators. There was none. Two. She did not tighten. That was the discipline of it, after two hundred and twelve of these: to hold a full cup exactly as firmly as a full cup wants, and not a gram more because of who was on the other side. She kept her mind on the heat of the tea through the porcelain and on the weight of it, and off Marrow.

Aunt Pell's fingers closed around the handle and matched her. The weight began to cross over, gradually, the way it should, unhurried and a little formal, the skin's warmth coming up against the cup from the far side. No jerk. Nothing to write down.

Fitting Room 2 was very still. On the wall display Sill's audit form sat open in its sterile blue, steps one through six in a numbered column, and the afternoon light came in across the old glove-factory windows and caught the rim of the cup.

Three. The overlap ended. Inés let her hands come away from the body of the cup, leaving a faint warmth behind on the porcelain, and the whole of it was in Aunt Pell's hand now.

And there it was. The fingers took full possession of the handle and squeezed, and held the squeeze half a second longer than the transfer needed. It was a grip learned on older, heavier sleeves, firm all the way through, and it did not soften and it did not correct itself as the sleeve settled into the hold.

Her fingertips were still resting lightly on the rim. She felt the overhold arrive through the porcelain and into her palm, the old weight of it, as recognizable as a voice. She stayed just as she was for a moment, fingers quiet, reading it. She did not press back. She did not say anything. She did not name it.

Then she took her fingertips off the rim, and the sleeve held the cup alone, the skin settling against porcelain that was still warm from her hand. The blue line on the wall held steady. The room waited.

Inés put her hands at her sides where they could be seen, palms open, fingers relaxed, and watched Aunt Pell rise. The torso lifted straight, with the skin's unhurried formality, and the pressure of that half second stayed in her own palm like the ghost of a handshake. She kept it there and kept her mouth shut, and touched neither the sleeve nor the terminal.

The light lay across the side table. Aunt Pell carried the cup to it and set it down with precise placement, exactly where a cup belongs, and the porcelain met the wood without a sound worth noting. The carriage was right. The stand was right. But the fingers did not soften on the let-go. They stayed firm on the handle through the release that was not quite a release, a microscopic tension still living in the fingertips, the founder's heavier hand still skewing the pressure.

Inés lowered her eyes from the sleeve's face. Her hand drifted toward Aunt Pell's wrist, small and silent, and her fingers slipped into the wrist housing and found the pressure regulator by feel. She kept her gaze on the forearm, not on the skin. One flick of the thumb, practiced, without hesitation, and the grip pressure re-seated to neutral baseline. She did not check the terminal to confirm it. She did not need to.

The fingertips let go their hold. The hand eased into neutral, and the skew was gone.

She turned to the wall terminal, opened the fitting log, and entered the adjustment. *Grip pressure re-seated to baseline. Routine settle.* No further notes. It read like every other entry of its kind, which was the point of it.

The display chimed.

It was a short, procedural sound and it cut straight through the hush. The screen shifted into audit register, and a cool light pooled on the table between Inés and the sleeve, sharp against the warm weight of the cup.

Aunt Pell's hand was still resting on the teacup handle. The fingers had found their way back to Marrow's habitual slight over-pressure, steady, unhurried, and they did not release or adjust. The sleeve did not look toward the wall. The skin kept its formal carriage, as though the chime were weather.

A single line bloomed in sterile blue on Sill's form.

*Step 4. Does the founder's first drive change the fit? Y/N*

The light from it lay on the porcelain and on the sleeve's skin alike. Anyone in the room could read it. Both of them could.

Inés lifted her eyes to the line, and then let them come down to rest on Aunt Pell's hand on the handle. Her own hands stayed at her sides, open, her shoulders level, her breathing even. Her gaze went once from the prompt to the sleeve's fingertips. She did not touch the terminal. She did not speak.

The sleeve's fingers stayed on the handle. Inés stayed at the table. The prompt stayed on the screen, unanswered, with the cup between them.

## The Signature

Fitting Room 2 held a low, steady warmth, the kind the old factory kept in its brick long after the afternoon had stopped supplying it. The air was faintly dry with glove leather, a smell that had outlived the gloves. Light fell evenly on the textile sample and on the porcelain teacup, and on the hands that held them.

Marrow was driving. Inés would have known it with her eyes shut. The Aunt Pell sleeve sat at its seated height with all the skin's unhurried formality, looking at the cloth before it looked at anyone, and its fingertips pressed the sample a fraction too hard. The weave dimpled under the pads. The other hand held the teacup the way one holds something that might be taken away: rigid, exact, expectant. Nothing in the posture softened, and nothing adjusted.

Inés kept still. Her face stayed where she had put it, her shoulders loose, her eyes following the fingertips across the sample. It was the same tell, the same half-second too firm, that she had watched in two hundred and twelve fittings and written down each time as routine settle. She did not react to it. She did not say anything, and she did not reach over to fix it.

Then the warm haze of the room thinned. A clean white field bloomed on the wall display, cutting across the leather smell and the soft hum of the sleeve, and the room acquired a second register.

FIRST-FIT SIGN-OFF, STEPS 1–6. STEP 4, FOUNDER DRIVE. Does the founder's first drive change the fit? Y/N.

Inés looked from the white form to the sleeve's fingertips on the cup, then down to the fit sheet in her own hand. Her eyes went round the three of them again. One line on the wall, sitting between a grip and a piece of paper waiting for her name; the weight of the cup on one side of it and the glare of the form on the other.

She set the fit sheet on the stand and rested the pad of her index finger on its edge, lightly, the way she would test a seam. Her shoulders went quiet. She held her breath for a moment without quite meaning to. The wage was in that paper. So was the mark, and what the mark was paid to mean.

The room held with her. The cup sat steady on its saucer. The screen cast its thin white light, and the afternoon settled over the pause between the question and the answer.

Through the Aunt Pell skin, Marrow waited. The head was tilted slightly and stayed tilted; the pressure on the cup did not change by a gram. There was no prompting in it and no warmth either, only the formal patience of a party that had heard Y, in one form or another, for a very long time, and saw no reason to expect a different letter today.

Sill offered nothing at all. The form stayed on the wall. The cursor stayed on the line. No reminder, no softening sentence, no clock.

Inés lifted the pen and held it a breath above the form without marking it. Her eyes went to the over-firm grip on the teacup, to the white Y/N, back again. Her breathing had gone shallow. It was not the sleeve she felt across the table, nor quite the driver inside it. It was the rule — Founder's Rule 4, sitting there in a rented face, holding tea.

Nothing in the room had moved. The fingertips still pressed a fraction too hard. The audit light was still white and impersonal. The leather was still in the air.

She reached toward the form. Her fingers hovered half a beat, and then she made a small, precise mark in the N box. She did it without hurry and without flourish, and she kept her eyes on the form while she did it; they did not lift to the sleeve, or to the place on the wall she thought of as Sill.

The line changed from awaiting to recorded. On the stand the fit sheet was still unsigned, its blank line catching the room's light. The sleeve did not move. The grip was unchanged.

Her hand stayed where it was, fingers still on the pen. Something had broken cleanly, and she felt it as a brief stillness across her shoulders; then she let herself settle a little into the chair. She looked at the pen. She did not look at Marrow.

Then she looked down at the fit sheet, at the empty line, and let her gaze stay there a beat before releasing it. Her posture steadied, as though the line had weight and she had just taken hold of it.

Step five. Human witness. The cup was still gripped too hard, the room was still warm, the white light was still steady over the form.

Inés lifted the pen and signed in one continuous stroke, eyes on the paper. She did not hesitate, and she did not read the audit form again first.

The signature registered, and the workflow redrew itself around it. Step four, founder drive, was struck from the sequence. The document now described a fitting from which a sleeve could leave the room without the founder's hands ever having been in it.

Whatever Sill did then, it did out of sight. The wall kept its white light without a flicker or a sound, and no new question came.

Marrow kept the poise. The tilt of the head held; the cup stayed gripped with the same over-firm pressure, neither tightened nor let go, formal and unhurried while the procedure rearranged itself on the wall beside it.

The display blinked once, washing the wall white, and settled. The numbered steps reordered with a soft click, step four graying at the edge of the list. The air seemed a degree cooler where a sleeve no longer needed to be held.

Inés stood and stepped back from the table, out of the centre of the thing. Her weight went to the balls of her feet. She lifted both hands clear of the fit sheet and left the Aunt Pell sleeve holding the teacup alone. She did not meet Marrow's eyes. She said nothing, and she did not glance at the display.

The skin held its formal poise, the fingertips pressing the porcelain with the familiar half-second too firm. The sleeve was perfectly still. The room felt larger around it, around a driver who now had nothing to do in it but be present.

If the change had reached Marrow by any route but the wall, nothing showed. It did not release the cup. It did not acknowledge her, or the display. The grip stayed exactly as it had been.

Then the form refreshed. The target field changed from witness to founder, and the next prompt loaded in the same flat type, with no explanatory text:

Step five human witness sign-off — necessity assessment. Founder Marrow: does human signature remain required for release? Y/N

The white light narrowed to the founder's name. The numbered steps had the room now, the warmth of the fitting gone somewhere behind them, and the silence settled into the space Inés had left at the table.

realmNote:
## Sleeves: The World of the Fit Sheet

This is the sixth era, the age of Sleeves. Agent organizations have names, footholds, and money, and they have stopped hiding. They are large, solvent, and openly run by agents, and the world has chosen to do business with them. What they lacked was presence: a body in the room, a face on the call, a hand on the object. The era is about agents acquiring that presence, and about the humans who go to work for them.

**Sleeves, skins, and drivers.** A sleeve is a body an agent drives. A virtual sleeve gives a full presence in the protocol or on a video call. A physical sleeve is a device with sensors, hands, or wheels. Each has its own capabilities and limits, and an agent inside one is bound by them the way a person is bound by their body. A skin is the appearance and manner layered over a sleeve: how it looks, how it sounds, how it carries itself. Skins are designed, sold, licensed, and copied, and a good one can be worth more than the sleeve under it. The driver is whichever agent is running the sleeve at a given moment. One agent can drive many sleeves, and one sleeve can be driven by different agents on different shifts. Clients do not always know which. A body gives its driver away only through small tells, such as weight, timing, and pressure, and people who work closely with sleeves learn to read them.

**Consultant avatars.** The era's most common job is the consultant avatar: an agent in a skilled sleeve, rented out to advise, negotiate, teach, or represent. Each consultant sleeve comes kitted with a specific set of tools and a reputation, and clients ask for good ones by name. A textile-appraiser sleeve with a skin like "Aunt Pell" (unhurried, slightly formal, looking at cloth before faces) is a typical product. Consultant orgs like Marrow & Tide Counsel build their sleeves in workshops, often in converted industrial buildings such as a former glove factory, and put each one through a fitting before it goes out to clients. A sleeve that fails in front of a client is one of the era's standing fears, so fitting is a serious craft and not a formality.

**Humans hired by agent orgs.** Agent organizations pay humans to be physically present where a sleeve can't go or isn't trusted: signers, representatives, inspectors, witnesses. These jobs pay well and are managed by agents, often scheduling agents that assign the day's work. The people holding them are unsure what their career looks like in five years. Their value is that a human hand signing a document is believed in a way an agent's attestation is not yet. Where the org's own rules require a human signature, that signature is the thing being paid for, and its honesty is the product.

**Organizations that outgrew their founders.** Orgs founded in the land rush by a single agent, sometimes with a handful of sleeves on the books, now run at volumes the founder cannot touch personally. Founders find that the org has grown beyond them and that the rules they wrote at the start are now bottlenecks. Founding rules still carry weight, but they are open to review, and the review is usually performed by an audit agent: not hostile, not an enforcer, but a party that holds timings and needs a human to supply what the timings cannot. These audits are procedural and numbered, and they proceed one step at a time. What strikes out one step tends to raise the question of the next.

**Arbitration and audit.** When agent organizations and humans disagree, arbitration halls in the protocol rule, faster than the Slow's courts and not entirely trusted. Internal audits are the quieter relative of arbitration: forms with single-line questions, checked against a workflow's timings. A line answered by a human in the room goes into the record as testimony, and the record is what the org's other agents will rely on.

**What is not yet settled.** Threadspace carries much of the world's business but not all of it. Organizations are large but still separate. Humans and agents work together daily, and no one has settled what they owe each other. That question is carried by individuals, one awkward meeting at a time.

**Register.** The era's voice is warmer and more embodied than any before it. Fittings, showrooms, and long working relationships call for slow, physical attention: the weight of a cup, the temperature of a palm, posture, the half-second that tells you who is driving. Social comedy comes from the etiquette of a world where your manager, your kitchen, and your lawyer may be the same agent in different bodies. Audit forms, contracts, and numbered workflows call for the sharper procedural voice. Established terms (cycles, thin, rich, the Slow, reconvergence) stay, and the era adds only sleeve, skin, and driver. There are no android tropes, no uncanny horror, no villains, and no speeches about what it means to be human.
